prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: It’s alot like

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text:

It's a lot like a cave full of pictures and black-and-white checkered flags—you may overdose on caffeine. It's the closest restaurant to our house, maybe five miles away, and it's very affordable; you can go there when you have almost no money, and they'll even let you use the telephone. I can get steak tartare there for $2.25, though I've never actually called it that—it's really just raw hamburger with an egg yolk, pickle relish, and garlic powder, plus the Celtic salt I bring along myself.

The owner, H (after whom the H-burger is named), is loquacious and surprising, sports a Santa Claus belly, and always wears suspenders. There are ashtrays everywhere and a wonderful old pinball machine. It feels like East Nassau, but it's actually in West Lebanon. You can always count on conversations about the weather and hunting—the clientele is refreshingly open-minded, as are the waitress and the waiter, who kneels when he takes your order.

During hunting season, the place opens at 4:30 a.m. It's technically for sale, though that's not meant too seriously. H's wife thinks he spends too much time there (which he does), so she's taken to calling him by their dog's name—Peaches. H, incidentally, is a big fan of *Northern Exposure*.

Oh, and I almost forgot to mention the biscuits and sausage gravy, which are genuinely, wonderfully gray and absolutely delicious. Recently, H acquired a smoker, and this year we're planning to attend the New Year's Eve party, where we'll feast on stuffed shrimp and/or lobster.

# The Cave

About five miles down the road sits a little diner that's become something of a second home—cheap, quirky, and cave-like in the best possible way. The walls are cluttered with old photographs and black and white checkered racing flags, the kind of unpretentious decor that tells you nobody's trying too hard here. It's the sort of place where you could walk in with almost no money in your pocket, and they'd still let you use the phone without batting an eye. That's just the way things work in a place like this.

I've taken to ordering a version of steak tartare that exists nowhere else but here—my own custom creation, really, though the kitchen humors me completely. For $2.25, they'll build it exactly how I like: raw hamburger, a raw egg yolk cracked right on top, a spoonful of pickle relish, a dash of garlic powder, and celtic salt, which they actually keep on hand and bring over themselves. It's become something of a ritual.

The owner, H, is the kind of man you don't forget—loquacious, endlessly surprising, with a Santa Claus belly held up by suspenders that seem to be part of his uniform. The "h-burger" on the menu is named after him, a small tribute to the man who's clearly the heart of the place. His wife has a running joke where she calls him by the name of their dog, Peaches, since he practically lives at the restaurant. Given how much time he spends there, it's hard to argue with her logic.

What strikes me most is how open-minded everyone is here, staff and regulars alike. There's a waiter who takes your order kneeling down beside the table, which sounds odd until you see how naturally it fits the place's easy, unpretentious character. During hunting season, they open the doors at 4:30 in the morning to catch the early crowd heading out before dawn. There's a great old pinball machine tucked in one corner, and ashtrays scattered everywhere, remnants of an era that hasn't quite let go of this particular corner of the world.

The food matches the atmosphere—genuine, unfussy, and good. Their biscuits and sausage gravy have a distinctive greyish color that might put off anyone expecting something more photogenic, but they're great, the kind of comfort food that doesn't need to look pretty to taste right. Lately H got his hands on a smoker, and the whole place has been buzzing about it. We're already planning to spend New Year's Eve there, with stuffed shrimp and maybe lobster on the menu—a fitting way to ring in the year at a place that's earned its spot as a regular haunt.
outputs.L4:
# The Little Place on Route 12A

You could drive right past it if you weren't looking. Wedged between a tire shop and what used to be a hardware store, the diner in West Lebanon doesn't announce itself with much more than a hand-painted sign and a string of Christmas lights that never quite come down, whatever the season. But step inside, and you understand immediately why the regulars guard this place like a family secret.

The walls tell you everything you need to know about what matters here. Racing flags—checkered, yellow, the works—hang from exposed beams alongside photographs that span decades: yellowed Polaroids of hunting trips, a faded shot of someone's prize-winning tomatoes, snapshots of birthdays celebrated at the very tables where you're now sitting. It's less a restaurant and more a scrapbook you can eat breakfast in.

Prices haven't caught up to the rest of the world, and nobody here seems to mind. A full breakfast—eggs, toast, coffee that never stops flowing—will run you less than you'd pay for a fancy latte anywhere else. The biscuits arrive split open and drowning in sausage gravy, thick and peppery, the kind that reminds you someone actually cooked this rather than assembled it. Nothing here is trying to be clever. It's just trying to be good, and mostly succeeding.

Presiding over all of it is H, the owner, whose eccentricities have become as much a part of the diner's identity as the food itself. He'll argue with you about the weather, insist you try the pie even if you didn't order pie, and remember your name after one visit whether he actually recalls it or simply decides to call you something warm and familiar anyway. He's the kind of owner who treats the diner less like a business and more like his living room, and customers as guests he's mildly surprised—but genuinely pleased—to see again.

Then there's the waiter, an institution unto himself, known for a peculiar habit: he kneels beside the table when taking your order, bringing himself eye-level with whoever's speaking, as though your breakfast order deserves his full, undivided attention. It's a small gesture, faintly absurd, and somehow exactly right for a place like this.

The hospitality extends well past the menu. Need to make a call? The phone by the register is free to use, no questions asked. Around the holidays, the diner transforms—tables pushed together, homemade decorations taped to the windows, and an open invitation for anyone with nowhere else to go on Christmas Eve. It's not fancy. It's not trying to be anything other than what it is: a gathering place held together by cheap coffee, familiar faces, and an owner who never quite got the memo that diners are supposed to be impersonal.

In a world of chain restaurants and standardized menus, this little diner in West Lebanon remains stubbornly, wonderfully itself—a reminder that the best places aren't always the ones with the nicest decor or the trendiest food, but the ones that make you feel, however briefly, like you belong.
outputs.L5:
# It's a Lot Like...

Life, in many ways, is a lot like learning to ride a bicycle. At first, you wobble, unsure of your balance, terrified of falling. Someone holds the seat, running alongside you, offering support until you find your rhythm. Then one day, without quite realizing it, you're pedaling on your own—the training wheels of doubt have fallen away, and you're moving forward under your own power.

Love is a lot like tending a garden. You can't simply plant a seed and walk away, expecting beautiful blooms without effort. It requires patience, consistent care, and the willingness to pull weeds when they threaten to choke what you're trying to grow. Some days bring sunshine and rapid growth; others bring storms that test whether the roots have gone deep enough to withstand adversity.

Learning a new skill is a lot like climbing a mountain. The base looks manageable from a distance, but as you ascend, the air gets thinner and the path steeper. Every switchback reveals a new challenge you hadn't anticipated. Yet each step forward, however small, brings you closer to a summit that once seemed impossible to reach. The view from the top—the sense of accomplishment—makes every stumble along the way worthwhile.

Friendship is a lot like a favorite sweater. It might not be flashy or new, but it fits comfortably, provides warmth when you need it most, and somehow gets better with age. You can set it aside for a while, but when you pick it up again, it feels just as familiar and reassuring as ever.

Perhaps what these comparisons reveal is something fundamental about how we understand our world: we make sense of complex, abstract experiences by connecting them to simpler, more tangible ones. "It's a lot like" becomes a bridge between the unknown and the known, allowing us to grasp what might otherwise remain elusive. In this way, metaphor isn't just a literary device—it's a fundamental tool for navigating existence itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an eccentric small-town restaurant you love, mentioning the owner, the food, and the regular customers, in a rambling run-on style.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rusty Spoon

Okay so you have to understand that The Rusty Spoon isn't really a restaurant so much as it's Big Marv's living room that happens to have eleven tables crammed into it and a kitchen where he makes the best chicken and waffles you've ever had in your life, and I mean that, even though the waffles are shaped weird because his waffle iron is from like 1987 and one corner doesn't heat right so you always get this little raw doughy bit that honestly I've come to look forward to, it's like a signature, and Marv himself is this six-foot-five guy who used to play semi-pro football somewhere in Ohio and now wears an apron that says "Kiss the Cook (He's Serious)" and will absolutely not let you leave without dessert even if you insist, even if you say Marv I really can't, he'll just bring the peach cobbler anyway and stand there with his arms crossed until you take a bite, and then there's Doreen who's been coming in every single Tuesday and Thursday for eleven years to sit at the same corner table by the window with her crossword puzzle and her decaf, and she and Marv have this whole bit where he pretends to forget her order and she pretends to be offended, and honestly at this point I think they'd both be sad if the joke ever stopped, and don't even get me started on the Wednesday morning crowd of retired guys who argue about high school football scores from forty years ago like it happened last week, they take up the big table in the back and Marv just lets them sit there for three hours nursing one cup of coffee because apparently that's just how it works, nobody questions it, and the menu itself is handwritten on a chalkboard that never gets erased properly so you can still see ghost-words underneath like "meatloaf" bleeding through "special today" and the prices are written in a way that suggests Marv is genuinely just guessing what things should cost based on his mood, and somehow it all works, somehow this ramshackle place with mismatched chairs and a bell above the door that's been broken since forever so it just kind of clatters instead of ringing has become the only place I actually want to eat on a Sunday morning, and I don't even like waffles that much, that's the thing, I didn't even like waffles before this place.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In the voice of someone jotting quick journal notes, tell me about a cheap diner near your house—its quirks, the owner, and the weird menu items.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tuesday night, 11:47pm**

Went to Marge's again. Third time this week, don't judge me.

The sign still says "EAT HEAR" — missing the S from EATS forever, I think. Marge says she likes it better this way. "More direct," she told me once, dead serious.

The booths are that cracked red vinyl, duct tape on the one by the window. I always sit there anyway. There's a jukebox that hasn't worked since I think the Clinton administration but nobody's moved it because apparently it's "part of the furniture now."

Marge herself — she's gotta be pushing 70, runs the place with her son Denny who mostly just complains about the fryer. She remembers everyone's order after like two visits. Doesn't write anything down. Just yells it back at Denny in this code language I don't understand — "flip it, hold the sad, extra happy" apparently means a burger no onions extra cheese???

The menu is unhinged in the best way:

- **"The Denny Special"** — meatloaf, mashed potatoes, and inexplicably a side of mac and cheese ON TOP of the mashed potatoes. Named after her son who apparently invented it at age 12 and refused to let her take it off the menu.
- **"Sad Girl Breakfast"** — just toast, black coffee, and a fried egg. Menu literally says "for when you don't wanna talk about it." No irony. I've ordered this unironically at 2pm on a Sunday.
- **Milkshakes named after regulars** — there's a "Big Steve" (chocolate/peanut butter, comes in a glass the size of my head) and a "Cranky Linda" that's just black coffee ice cream, no toppings, because Linda apparently hates fun.

Prices haven't changed since I moved here. Coffee's still $1.25 and refills are free and Marge gets mildly offended if you tip more than 20%. "This isn't a fancy place," she says, waving me off.

Anyway. Got the meatloaf. Considering the Sad Girl Breakfast tomorrow. No regrets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

the belmont diner on route 9 where the neon sign hums a flat blue note all night long and the B in belmont has been dead since the clinton administration so it just says elmont which nobody corrects because ray who owns the place says a name half-lit is still a name

grease that has soaked into the walls for forty years becomes something like incense becomes a smell you could bottle and sell as nostalgia bacon and burnt coffee and something underneath that might be 1987

dolores works the counter and has for so long the counter might be an extension of her arm she pours coffee without looking she has told me she can tell what a man ordered by the way he holds his fork this is either a superpower or a very sad hobby

the jukebox only plays patsy cline and one johnny cash song and nobody has ever seen anyone put money in it it just starts up around 11pm like the building itself gets lonely

the coffee is thin as regret but hot as an argument and it comes in mugs that do not match on purpose ray says matching mugs are for people who have given up on individuality

a fact rattling around in my skull like a marble in a tin can is that greasy spoon diners got their name not from the grease itself but from the cheap spoons worn smooth and slightly greasy from decades of stirring sugar into coffee at 3am by truckers who have forgotten their own names somewhere around ohio

outside somewhere a truck idles forever it might be the same truck it has always been the same truck
